name: GFlowNets (Generative Flow Networks) for Combinatorial Generation
key_paper: Bengio et al., 'Flow Network based Generative Models for Non-Iterative Diverse Candidate Generation', NeurIPS 2021; Malkin et al., 'Trajectory Balance: Improved Credit Assignment in GFlowNets', NeurIPS 2022
algorithm_description: GFlowNets learn a stochastic policy that generates discrete combinatorial objects by sequentially building them step-by-step through a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where each complete trajectory corresponds to one generated object. The key principle is that the learned policy samples objects proportionally to a reward function R(x) — i.e., high-reward objects are sampled more frequently but not exclusively, preserving diversity. Training uses a flow-matching objective: the Trajectory Balance (TB) objective (Malkin et al. 2022) requires that for any complete trajectory tau = (s0, s1, ..., sn), the product of forward policy probabilities times a learned initial flow Z equals the product of backward policy probabilities times the reward R(sn). This TB objective provides much lower variance gradients than the original detailed balance or flow-matching objectives, making it substantially more stable on small datasets. The forward policy, backward policy, and scalar log Z are all jointly optimized via standard gradient descent.
action_space_handling: GFlowNets use a sequential, autoregressive action space where each action extends the partially constructed object by one element. At each step, the forward policy P_F(s' | s) defines a distribution over valid next states (or a terminal action). The action space is naturally factored — at step t, only elements not yet selected are valid actions, enforcing distinctness. The flow through the DAG is not enumerated explicitly; only the forward policy network and backward policy network are parameterized (typically as neural networks sharing an encoder). This makes the effective action space O(N) per step rather than O(C(N, k)), which is critical for tractability.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: A set of k distinct numbers from {1..N} is formed autoregressively: starting from an empty set s0, at each step t the forward policy selects one number from the remaining unchosen candidates ({1..N} minus already-chosen numbers). After k steps, a terminal action is taken and the complete set is returned as the output. Masking is applied at each step to zero out already-selected numbers before computing softmax, guaranteeing that all k chosen numbers are distinct. This is structurally identical to pointer-network-style autoregressive selection but trained via flow objectives rather than supervised imitation or REINFORCE.
sequential_generation_strategy: Fully autoregressive — numbers are generated one at a time, each conditioned on all previously selected numbers in the current partial set. This means GFlowNets can model inter-number correlations (e.g., certain pairs co-occurring more often in high-reward draws) unlike flat multi-hot methods. The generation order within a set is typically treated as unordered (the DAG merges permutations of the same set into the same terminal state), which reduces the effective DAG size and improves training efficiency. Order-agnostic training (Shi et al. 2022) explicitly exploits this by averaging over multiple orderings.
gradient_estimator_type: GFlowNets do not use REINFORCE or reparameterization in the standard sense. The Trajectory Balance objective is a regression loss: log P_F(tau) + log Z - log P_B(tau) - log R(x) is minimized in squared-error form. Gradients flow through the forward and backward policy networks directly (no discrete sampling in the gradient path — the TB loss is computed on completed trajectories sampled from the current policy, then treated as supervised regression targets). This makes GFlowNet training lower-variance than REINFORCE and avoids the non-differentiability issues of Gumbel-softmax. The tradeoff is that Z (partition function estimate) must be learned simultaneously, adding one scalar parameter.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Distinctness of the k selected numbers is enforced via autoregressive masking: at each generation step, the logits for already-selected numbers are set to -infinity before softmax, making re-selection impossible. The exact set size k is enforced by running exactly k selection steps before forcing the terminal action. No rejection sampling is needed. This is a hard constraint rather than a soft penalty, so invalid outputs (duplicates or wrong cardinality) are structurally impossible.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium — GFlowNets are more sample-efficient than vanilla policy gradient methods on combinatorial tasks because the TB objective provides lower-variance training signal and the flow-matching framework naturally smooths the reward landscape. However, they still require enough complete trajectory rollouts to estimate Z accurately. On datasets of fewer than 200 draws, GFlowNets face the challenge that the reward model itself (trained on historical lottery data) is unreliable, which propagates noise into the flow objective. Empirically, GFlowNets have shown strong results on molecular generation tasks with hundreds of training points, suggesting medium suitability for this regime.
regularization_built_in: The TB objective implicitly regularizes via the partition function Z, which acts as a normalization constant and prevents the policy from collapsing to a single mode. The backward policy P_B (often set to uniform over orderings) provides additional implicit regularization by spreading probability mass. Entropy-based exploration can be added explicitly as an entropy bonus on P_F. Unlike Actor-Critic methods, there is no value baseline that could overfit. Temperature scaling on the reward R(x)^beta (beta < 1 flattens, beta > 1 sharpens) provides explicit diversity control analogous to a KL penalty.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1) Z estimation instability: the learned scalar log Z can drift significantly when training data is sparse, causing the TB loss to oscillate rather than converge. 2) Reward model overfitting: when the reward is provided by a neural network trained on <200 samples, GFlowNets will faithfully learn to oversample the overfit reward peaks, amplifying rather than correcting the underlying model's errors. 3) Backward policy mismatch: if the backward policy P_B is trained (rather than set to uniform), it can overfit on small data and produce inconsistent flow estimates. 4) Mode collapse to high-reward memorized sets: if the reward landscape has a few sharp peaks from the training data, the policy concentrates on those specific sets rather than exploring the combinatorial space.
data_regime_evidence: The original GFlowNet papers (Bengio et al. 2021, Malkin et al. 2022) primarily validate on molecular generation (drug discovery) with hundreds to thousands of candidate molecules evaluated per training run — the data regime is not directly comparable to fixed historical lottery draws. Lahlou et al. (2023) 'A Theory of Continuous Generative Flow Networks' and Pan et al. (2023) 'Better Training of GFlowNets with Local Credit and Incomplete Trajectories' touch on small-batch regimes but do not report results below 200 training samples explicitly. [uncertain: minimum_training_samples_tested] The closest analog is Shen et al. (2023) on set generation with ~500 training samples. No published GFlowNet paper as of mid-2025 specifically benchmarks on fewer than 200 fixed offline examples with a pre-trained reward model.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: [uncertain] No finite-sample convergence guarantees exist for GFlowNets as of 2025. The TB objective has been shown to be equivalent to a regression problem with a well-defined minimum, and Deleu et al. (2022) 'Bayesian Structure Learning with Generative Flow Networks' provides some theoretical grounding for convergence to the target distribution under infinite data, but finite-sample bounds analogous to PAC-MDP results for MDPs have not been established. Empirical convergence on small datasets is sensitive to the learning rate for log Z and the choice of backward policy.
reward_distribution_handling: GFlowNets are specifically designed to handle multi-modal, skewed reward distributions — in fact, this is their primary motivation over mode-seeking methods like beam search or standard RL. They sample proportionally to R(x), so rare high-reward plays are sampled with frequency proportional to their reward rather than being either ignored (as in mode-seeking) or equally weighted (as in uniform sampling). For lottery's ~95% zero-hit reward: the zero-reward terminal states will collectively receive near-zero flow under the learned policy, concentrating probability mass on the small fraction of historically rewarded number combinations. Minimum draws for stable learning is [uncertain] but likely 50-100 complete trajectories with non-zero reward signal.
credit_assignment_granularity: GFlowNets naturally provide step-level credit assignment since each step in the autoregressive generation corresponds to selecting one number. The TB objective propagates reward credit backward through the entire trajectory. However, in the lottery context where reward is only available at the play level (did the full set of 7 numbers win?), GFlowNets operate at play-level credit assignment by default. If semi-bandit feedback is available (knowing which individual numbers hit), it can be incorporated by designing intermediate rewards at each selection step, but this requires custom reward shaping and is not the standard GFlowNet setup.
diversity_mechanism: Diversity is the core design principle of GFlowNets: by training the policy to sample proportionally to R(x) rather than argmax R(x), they structurally prevent mode collapse to a single play. Multiple plays sampled from the learned policy will cover different high-reward regions of the combinatorial space. Additional diversity can be controlled via reward temperature: using R(x)^beta with beta < 1 flattens the distribution toward more uniform sampling, beta = 1 gives exact proportional sampling, and beta > 1 concentrates on top-reward sets. No explicit diversity penalty or population-based mechanism is needed.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: GFlowNets are compatible with offline training from a fixed historical dataset, but with important caveats. The reward function R(x) must be defined without environment interaction — in lottery-nn this would be a reward model trained on historical draws (e.g., frequency-based scoring or the existing neural network's predicted probability). The GFlowNet policy is then trained to sample proportionally to this fixed reward model. This is a form of offline RL / reward-conditioned generation. No live draw results are needed during GFlowNet training itself. However, the quality of the learned policy is entirely bounded by the quality of the reward model, which is particularly problematic for lottery prediction where the true reward (future draws) is unknowable from historical data alone.
key_dependencies: No standard production-ready GFlowNet library exists as of 2025 beyond research codebases. The GFlowNet Foundation library (github.com/recursionpharma/gflownet) from Recursion Pharma is the most maintained reference implementation. Alternatively, torchrl (PyTorch) provides some primitives. Core dependency is PyTorch only, but integrating the TB objective, backward policy, and log Z estimation requires ~300-500 lines of custom code. No stable-baselines3 or Pyro dependency needed.
estimated_lines_of_code: 400-600 lines — forward policy network (reusing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder, ~50 lines), backward policy (uniform or learned MLP, ~80 lines), TB loss computation (~60 lines), trajectory rollout sampler with masking (~100 lines), log Z parameter + optimizer (~20 lines), reward model interface (~50 lines), training loop (~100 lines), integration hooks into main_swarm.py (~100 lines)
transfer_learning_compatibility: High compatibility — the forward policy P_F can be initialized from the existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder, treating it as a sequence encoder that conditions each autoregressive selection step on the current partial set and the draw history context. The encoder outputs a context vector; at each step t, a selection head (small MLP) maps context + partial-set embedding to logits over {1..N} with masking. This means Phase 1's pretrained backbone weights are directly reusable, and only the selection head and log Z need to be trained from scratch. The backward policy is typically set to uniform over orderings (no new parameters), making the transfer lightweight.
specific_application_in_project: In lottery-nn, GFlowNets would replace the current temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py with a learned generative policy that samples plays proportionally to a reward model. Concretely: (1) define a reward function R(play) as a combination of historical frequency score and the SharedLotteryTransformer's predicted probability for each number combination; (2) train a GFlowNet forward policy on top of the frozen SharedLotteryTransformer encoder to sample 7-number sets (LottoMax) or 6-number sets (6/49) proportionally to R; (3) at prediction time, sample 5-10 candidate plays from P_F and return them. This would apply to all three lotteries using per-lottery output heads. The primary benefit over current sampling is structured diversity with reward-proportional sampling rather than independent per-number sampling that ignores set-level statistics. Recommended for Phase 3 given implementation complexity; Phase 2 should use Actor-Critic first.
replaces_or_extends: Replaces temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py — the GFlowNet forward policy becomes the play generator, producing complete 7/6/5-number sets autoregressively rather than sampling each number independently from a predicted probability vector
existing_open_source_implementations: 1) gflownet (Recursion Pharma): github.com/recursionpharma/gflownet — most maintained, supports molecular graph generation, TB and DB objectives, PyTorch; 2) torchgfn: github.com/saleml/torchgfn — clean minimal implementation of GFlowNet objectives including TB, actively maintained as of 2024; 3) GFlowNet-FoundationModels: github.com/yoshuasusanto/GFlowNet — research code from Bengio group; 4) gfn-energy: github.com/GFNOrg/gfn-energy — continuous GFlowNets. The torchgfn library is the recommended starting point for new implementations due to its clean API and PyTorch-native design.
benchmark_results: Bengio et al. 2021 (NeurIPS): GFlowNet outperforms MCMC and genetic algorithms on molecular generation (GDB-8 dataset), generating 75%+ diverse top-k molecules vs. ~25% for mode-seeking baselines. Malkin et al. 2022 (NeurIPS, Trajectory Balance): TB objective achieves 2-5x lower variance gradients than Detailed Balance on hypergrid and sequence generation tasks, converges in ~50% fewer steps. Jain et al. 2022 'Biological Sequence Design with GFlowNets': strong results on DNA/protein sequence generation with ~1000 labeled examples, outperforming RL baselines on diversity metrics. No direct benchmarks on lottery-style combinatorial generation or datasets below 200 training examples.
notable_use_cases: 1) Drug/molecule discovery (primary domain): generating diverse drug candidates proportionally to predicted binding affinity — structurally similar to lottery (combinatorial discrete object, sparse high-reward signal, diversity requirement); 2) Causal structure learning (Deleu et al. 2022): learning Bayesian network DAG structures as sets of edges — direct analog of selecting a set of numbers; 3) Scientific hypothesis generation: Jain et al. 2023 on biological sequence design with limited labeled data; 4) Combinatorial optimization: Pan et al. 2023 apply GFlowNets to TSP and set cover problems, showing competitive performance vs. learned heuristics; 5) Crystal structure generation: Kim et al. 2024 on materials science with limited experimental data — closest analog to small-data lottery regime
